prompt.context: Kyle's Brick Company manufactures, distributes, and sells bricks to a wide variety of clients in the southeastern United States. They have historically grown by approximately 7% per year. They have recently experienced flat growth and have asked for your recommendations.
prompt.question: Why has growth gone flat and what do you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: Is this profit or revenue growth at 7%?
clarifying_info.a: Their margins (as a percentage) have grown slightly over the past 5 years. The growth they are seeking to resume is revenue growth and not profitability.

clarifying_info.q: Has their growth historically been through new customers or same customers?
clarifying_info.a: Both. They have expanded conservatively through geographic expansion as well as increasing same customer sales.

clarifying_info.q: Have they changed anything about their selling process?
Have they lost any major clients?
clarifying_info.a: No. The client portfolio has been expanding at expected levels and no major clients have been lost over the last year.
No. The overall market for bricks has grown at 5% the past 2 years.
Costs on a per unit basis have declined slightly over the past 2 years.
No. There is a large number of backlogged orders due to insufficient factory production.

clarifying_info.q: Have competitors or clients changed anything about their processes?
clarifying_info.a: No. Bricks are a commodity and quality across competitors is similar.

clarifying_info.q: What does the value chain look like?
clarifying_info.a: Raw materials come in and are formed in a molding machine, treated with chemicals at treating, and then baked and packaged. The bottleneck has been confirmed to be located at baking.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cycle time of the baking machine?
clarifying_info.a: It can handle 16 batches per day.

clarifying_info.q: How many hours does the facility operate?
Does the baking machine experience downtime?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the current utilization is around 60%. The baking machine typically outputs 9.6 batches per day against a potential output of 16 batches/day.

clarifying_info.q: Does the baking have significant yield loss?
Has the baking machine changed over time?
clarifying_info.a: No, the output has been consistent over the past 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: Why is the machine utilization so low?
clarifying_info.a: Machine utilization is at 60% because the machine can handle 1000 bricks per batch, but there is tremendous variation in the loading amount due to operator preference. (provide Exhibit 2)

exhibits.title: Revenue and Profitability
exhibits.shows: A table showing annual Revenue, Profit Margin, Bricks Produced (tons), and Variable Costs for 2011–2014

exhibits.title: Brick Load of Baking Machine Histogram
exhibits.shows: A histogram of the relative frequency of bricks loaded per batch at the baking machine, with load sizes from 100 to 1000 bricks

data.note: Provide only if candidate specifically asks about the loading process at the baking machine

framework: Diagnose revenue driver: confirm flat revenue is a supply constraint, not a demand or pricing issue
Rule out demand-side issues: market growth, customer losses, competitive dynamics, pricing changes
Rule out sales/process changes: no change in selling process or client portfolio
Identify supply-side bottleneck: manufacturing output capped at 3700 tons/year with backlogged orders
Analyze cost structure: decompose revenue, variable costs, fixed costs to understand profit vs. capacity trade-off
Drill into factory operations: map value chain (molding → treating → baking → packaging) and isolate the baking bottleneck
Assess baking machine capacity: evaluate theoretical capacity, utilization rate, and yield
Determine if new capital expenditure is required or if operational improvement can unlock capacity

questions.prompt: Question 1: Why have sales stayed flat? Where would you like to investigate next?
questions.guidance: Strong answers rule out demand-side causes (market is growing 5%, no major client losses, no competitor issues) and identify an internal supply constraint. The candidate should hypothesize that manufacturing capacity is the bottleneck given backlogged orders and flat output. Mentioning declining unit cost as evidence of stable variable costs but under-investment in fixed/capital assets elevates the answer.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What conclusions can you reach from Exhibit 1? Push the candidate to calculate fixed costs for 2012 and 2013 and share insights.
questions.guidance: Strong answers note that revenue flattened while profit margin rose. Variable cost per ton is stable ($10/ton each year), suggesting distribution and labor are under control. The candidate should calculate fixed costs (Revenue x Margin - Variable Costs) and observe fixed costs per unit declining, indicating under-investment in capital assets to boost short-term profit at the expense of capacity expansion.

math.setup: Fixed Costs = Revenue - Variable Costs - Profit. Profit = Revenue x Profit Margin. Fixed Costs/Unit = Fixed Costs / Bricks Produced (tons).
steps: 2014: Same as 2013 — fixed costs flat at 18.5M, capacity has not grown
math.answer: Fixed costs per unit declined from $0.006 to $0.005 per ton from 2011 to 2013, suggesting fixed asset investment has not kept pace with volume growth. Capacity has stalled at 3700 tons since 2013.

questions.prompt: Question 3: The factory manager says maximum capacity is 3700 tons/year due to the baking process. We suspect the machine may have additional capacity. What would you want to know? Once the candidate identifies a utilization issue, provide Exhibit 2 and ask them to calculate the utilization rate.
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify the three components of output: actual cycle time, yield, and utilization. The candidate should ask about throughput, downtime, and loading consistency. Upon seeing Exhibit 2 they should calculate weighted-average utilization (~59.5%) and recognize that inconsistent operator loading is the root cause — the machine has theoretical capacity of ~6218 tons/year, far above current output of 3700 tons. Note: Exhibit 2 should be provided ONLY if the candidate specifically asks about utilization or the loading process at the baking step.

math.setup: Utilization per batch = Load / 1000 (machine capacity). Weighted utilization = SUMPRODUCT(Relative Frequency, Utilization). Theoretical Capacity = Current Volume / Utilization.
math.answer: Baking machine utilization is ~59.5%. Theoretical capacity is ~6218 tons/year — well above the 3700 tons currently produced and sufficient to meet demand without buying new equipment.

questions.prompt: Question 4: What recommendations would you make? Should our client buy another brick baking machine?
questions.guidance: Strong answers conclude that no new capital expenditure is needed. The recommendation should focus on standardizing the loading process to reduce operator variation and increase utilization. The candidate should acknowledge the risk that there may be a legitimate process reason for variation and recommend further investigation with operators and engineers before full implementation.

recommendation: Do not purchase a new baking machine — the existing machine has theoretical capacity of ~6218 tons/year vs. current output of 3700 tons
Implement standardized work at the baking machine loading step to reduce operator variation in batch size and increase utilization from ~60% toward 100%
This operational improvement should unlock sufficient capacity to fulfill backlogged orders and resume revenue growth
risks: There may be a legitimate process or quality reason for the inconsistent loading patterns (e.g., brick defect rates vary by load size), which would constrain the improvement opportunity
Operator resistance to standardized work may slow implementation
If standardized loading reveals a different bottleneck downstream, additional analysis will be needed
next_steps: Conduct time-and-motion study and interviews with baking machine operators and process engineers to understand root cause of loading variation
Pilot standardized loading protocol and measure impact on throughput and quality
Assess whether distribution capacity can absorb incremental volume once manufacturing output increases
